claim_review_provenance.scope: One qualitative pass over all eight saved biographies against the numbered saved Wikipedia input. No outside historical verification, Qwen self-review, or edits to generated text.
claim_review_provenance.claim_unit: Checkable factual propositions, separating nationality, occupations, dates, places and material relational qualifiers. Enumerations explicitly covered by one passage can form one proposition. Pure evaluative adjectives such as groundbreaking, monumental, influential and significant are not separately scored. The denominator depends on this annotation policy and is not a benchmark accuracy score.

status_definitions.supported: The full proposition is entailed by the saved input.
status_definitions.partial: The core is supported but a qualifier, generalization or causal relationship is not established.
status_definitions.unsupported: The saved input does not entail the proposition, or the stated detail conflicts with the relevant passage. This does not establish falsehood outside the input.
status_definitions.source_inconsistent: One saved passage supports the proposition but another saved passage materially conflicts with it.

claim_review_provenance.limitations: A single agent-assisted annotation pass, without independent human raters or inter-annotator agreement. Labels are qualitative and relative to the saved input; they are not automatic entailment measurements or independently verified historical truth.

items.name: Otto Hahn
items.summary: Otto Hahn was a German chemist and pioneer in radiochemistry who discovered isotopes of radium, thorium, protactinium, and uranium. A graduate of Marburg University, he earned his doctorate there in 1901 for a dissertation on bromine derivatives. After studying under Ernest Rutherford in Canada, Hahn returned to Germany in 1906. He worked with Lise Meitner at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry, where they made groundbreaking discoveries, including the isolation of a protactinium isotope in 1918. Hahn published over 250 scientific papers, contributing significantly to the field of radiochemistry.

items.name: Robert Bunsen
items.summary: Robert Wilhelm Eberhard Bunsen was a German chemist born in Göttingen in 1811. He studied with notable scientists like Gauss and Liebig before becoming a professor at the University of Marburg. There, he developed the Bunsen burner with his assistant Peter Desaga in 1855. Later, he discovered caesium and rubidium by analyzing mineral water from Dürkheim. His work on emission spectra led to the creation of the Bunsen-Kirchhoff Award. Bunsen also created the Bunsen cell battery and studied photochemistry extensively.

items.name: Emil von Behring
items.summary: Emil von Behring was a German physiologist who revolutionized medicine by developing serum therapy against diphtheria and tetanus. He won the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1901 for this work, earning him the title 'saviour of children' as diphtheria was a major cause of child death. After studying medicine in Berlin, he passed a state examination qualifying him to practice in the Marburg district. In 1895, he became Professor of Hygienics within the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Marburg, a position he held for the rest of his life. He founded the Behringwerke in Marburg to produce antitoxins and vaccines.

items.name: Jacob Grimm
items.summary: Jacob Ludwig Karl Grimm (1785–1863) was a German author, linguist, and folklorist. He studied law at the University of Marburg in 1802, where his brother Wilhelm joined him a year later. Together, they wrote Grimms' Fairy Tales and the monumental Deutsches Wörterbuch, a German language dictionary started in 1838. They also published German Legends and collected folktales from oral sources and manuscripts. Grimm discovered alliteration in ancient poems and published editions of legal traditions and Eddaic songs. His work on poetry in law and Germanic legal antiquities remains significant today.

items.name: Hannah Arendt
items.summary: Hannah Arendt (1906–1975) was a German and American historian and philosopher, one of the most influential political theorists of the twentieth century. Born in Linden to a Jewish family, she studied at the University of Marburg under Martin Heidegger, with whom she engaged in a romantic affair. She obtained her doctorate in philosophy at the University of Heidelberg in 1929, with her dissertation entitled Love and Saint Augustine. Her works cover a broad range of topics, but she is best known for those dealing with the nature of wealth, power, fame, and evil, as well as politics, direct democracy, authority, tradition, and totalitarianism.

items.name: K. Ferdinand Braun
items.summary: Karl Ferdinand Braun was a German physicist born in 1850 who studied at the University of Marburg before earning his Ph.D. He is known as the 'father of television' for inventing the first cathode-ray tube in 1897. Braun also developed the first semiconductor diode and shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Guglielmo Marconi for their work on wireless telegraphy. His two-circuit system made long-range radio transmissions possible, and his phased array antenna invention led to radar. He co-founded Telefunken and made significant contributions to modern electronics and communications technology.

items.name: Alfred Wegener
items.summary: Alfred Lothar Wegener (1880–1930) was a German scientist known for pioneering polar research and proposing the continental drift hypothesis in 1912. He worked at the University of Marburg as a lecturer in meteorology and applied astronomy until World War I, where his clear explanations were highly valued by students and colleagues. His lectures formed the basis of a standard meteorology textbook. Wegener later led an expedition to Greenland, where he and a Greenlander companion made a perilous journey to West camp, though they never reached it. He died around 90 miles from their camp in 1931, believed to have succumbed to heart failure from overexertion.

items.name: Boris Pasternak
items.summary: Boris Pasternak (1890–1960) was a Russian poet and novelist who began composing at age 13. Initially aspiring to be a musician, he briefly studied at the Moscow Conservatory before leaving abruptly in 1910 to study philosophy at the University of Marburg in Germany. There, he studied under prominent neo-Kantian philosophers. After returning to Moscow, he joined the Russian Futurist group Centrifuge as a pianist. His first book of poems, My Sister, Life, was published in Berlin in 1922 and soon became an important collection in the Russian language.
